articles.title: Ticker: Paula Reid Joins MS NOW as Chief White House Reporter
articles.fullContent:
By Mark Mwachiro Top of the Ticker : MS NOW has made it official, hiring Paula Reid as chief White House reporter. Reid, who begins her new role immediately, was previously at CNN, where she was chief legal affairs correspondent.

In a internal memo welcoming Reid, MS NOW Washington bureau chief Sudeep Reddy said, “Paula will bring her deep experience to covering the administration, serve as a key reporting voice across MS NOW’s Washington Bureau, and help drive our newsroom’s investigative and enterprise journalism.”

Access fight : CNN, MS NOW, and Politico amended their lawsuit concerning White House press access, asking U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly to make existing access orders permanent as well as prevent the White House from blocking them from performing their rotating press pool duties in the Oval Office and traveling on Air Force One.

New venture : Former CNN executive Andrew Morse has launched a new company, Phareo, which he describes as a “new platform to help creators find the audiences they deserve and to help fans find their next favorite creator.” Co-founded alongside Brian Whitman , Phareo seeks to challenge YouTube among other platforms in the creator ecosystem. Morse departed CNN in 2022 and was most recently the CEO of The Atlanta Journal-Constitution.

In her own words : CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss spoke publicly for the first time since taking over the news outlet at Jessica Lessin ’s The Information 2026 WTF Summit. Some of her remarks from the summit : There isn’t a crisis in trust but “a crisis in trustworthiness.” She also said that 60 Minutes is doing “tremendously well” and that she is not focused on the show’s weekly ratings.

Refreshed look : Regular viewers of ABC’s streaming network ABC News Live will have noticed the debut of a redesigned on-air graphics package. The refresh, which uses cleaner typography and sharper rendering, has the lower third center-justified with no backplate, a layout that works in both 16:9 and 9:16 and lets content move seamlessly into vertical video without reformatting.

Historical series : Landman actor Billy Bob Thornton is teaming with Fox Nation on a three-part historical docudrama, Billy Bob Thornton Presents: The Mayflower, premiering Nov. 23. The series traces the Pilgrims’ perilous Atlantic crossing aboard the Mayflower.

Wedding Bells : Two Fox News personalities recently tied the knot. Primetime host Sean Hannity married Fox & Friends co-host Ainsley Earhardt on Oct. 24. The ceremony was held at the Church of Bethesda-by-the-Sea in Palm Beach, Fla. Fellow colleagues at the celebration included Fox News Media CEO Suzanne Scott, on-air personalities Steve Doocy , Lawrence Jones , Brian Kilmeade , Laura Ingraham , and Bret Baier .

Revolving Door: Jon Carras has been promoted to senior producer of CBS Sunday Morning with Jane Pauley . Carras has been with the broadcast for 20 years, producing more than 400 stories for the CBS News Sunday morning news program.

NBC News has named Kevin Delaney its head of digital content and subscription. In this newly created role, Delaney will “work to develop content to support new opportunities that drive audience and revenue growth,” said Catherine Kim , executive vice president of editorial and content, and Sat Brainch , chief business officer, in a memo to staffers provided to Deadline . He has previously worked at The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and The Information.

Former 60 Minutes executive producer Bill Owens is joining Newspress as an executive producer. Owens will oversee the launch of new shows from the video journalism startup.

Honors : CNN chief medical correspondent Dr. Sanjay Gupta was inducted into the Atlanta Press Club Hall of Fame, recognizing his lasting impact on journalism, which included his quarter century career at CNN.

— CNN Communications (@CNNPR) October 30, 2026

articles.title: How Brands Like Wendy’s and Planet Fitness Wove Into the Fabric of Bravo Fan Fest
articles.fullContent:
By Bianca Brutus This year’s Bravo Fan Fest was so eventful, even a Haitian mortician was there.

Bravo Fan Fest returned to Charleston, SC on October 24, after debuting in Miami in 2024. There was live stage programming, branded activations, and photo ops with Bravolebrities from a number of hit shows, including Below Deck, The Real Housewives franchise, Southern Charm, Southern Hospitality, and Summer House.

ADWEEK spent the day on the ground of the festival, which is smaller and more intimate and community-driven that larger-scale events like BravoCon.

This year, the event had five brand sponsors: Colgate Optic White, Planet Fitness, State Farm, Wayfair, and Wendy’s. Each put real thought into how the audience would want to engage with their activations, finding ways to get them involved and focusing more on the shows fans love than their own products.

“Each partnership brings the brand into the Bravo world through familiar Easter eggs and fan-favorite moments, in a way that lets both the brand and the IP shine,” said Sari Feinberg, svp of marketing and brand partnerships at NBCUniversal Advertising and Partnerships.

At Colgate’s activation, attendees could play a giant toothbrush game to win prizes. There was also a smile-ready photo spot with a power fan, meant to make attendees feel like a Bravo main character. Visitors could also customize a travel bag with Colgate Optic White products.

Planet Fitness had hydration stations where attendees grabbed co-branded water bottles and scanned a hang tag to unlock one free month of the PF Black Card, which gives access to all clubs nationwide plus perks like hydromassages and exclusive app workouts.

State Farm, meanwhile, built a waterfront photo op inspired by Southern Charm. Cast members including Shep Rose and Madison LeCroy stopped by to pose with fans, while fans received customizable tote bags and could pick a scarf to match.

Wayfair’s activation was a big hit with Summer House fans. There, they could pose as a DJ, like the show’s star Kyle Cooke, next to cardboard cutouts of the cast. Fans also got to the chance to meet cast memeber Mia Calabrese and left with gift boxes that had a shoppable QR code for deals.

Wendy’s brought its BFF (Burgers, Fries, and Frosty) deal to an outdoor food truck. The fast-food chain also debuted two new Frosty flavors inspired by The Real Housewives of Rhode Island’s Alicia Carmody and The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City’s Lisa Barlow. Inside, fans could check in at The Real Housewives Ultimate Girls Trip Hotel, designed to feel like a real housewives trip.

Barlow’s Baby Gorgeous Meal is still available in the Wendy’s app and on DoorDash.

Kim Francella, svp of brand partnerships at NBCUniversal Advertising and Partnerships, views Fan Fest as an ongoing strategy to cultivate fandom. The intentionally intimate setting is key to building deeper connections that drive brand involvement.

“What we’re seeing is a true flywheel: the passion of the Bravo fanbase continues to drive incredible demand from brands,” said Francella.

While Bravoholics came for their favorite stars, they stayed for the experiences that seamlessly wove themselves into the festival.

Bianca Brutus currently serves as the Social Media Editor at ADWEEK. Her writing has appeared in NBC News, People Magazine, and The Knockturnal, among other publications. She is a major fan of greek yogurt and trinkets.

articles.title: How News Networks are Covering the 2026 Midterm Elections
articles.fullContent:
By Mark Mwachiro The 2026 midterm elections on Tuesday, Nov. 3 are shaping up to be one of the most consequential U.S. races in years.

This cycle has taken on the importance of a presidential election, with Democrats hoping it will serve as a referendum on Donald Trump ‘s presidency as they anticipate recapturing control of the House and the Senate. Meanwhile, Republicans hope their efforts are convincing enough to retain one, if not both, chambers of Congress.

News networks are offering extensive coverage across channels on Tuesday, with reporters stationed in key states and anchors in the studio using the latest technology to share the results.

Here is a rundown of what each network has planned.

World News Tonight’s David Muir will lead seven hours of coverage beginning at 7 p.m. ET, featuring its powerhouse political team including Linsey Davis , Martha Raddatz , Jonathan Karl , Mary Bruce , Pierre Thomas , Rachel Scott , and more.

Anchors, correspondents, and reporters from ABC News and ABC Owned Television Stations will be stationed across the country, with on-the-ground reporting on 11 crucial election states.

Wall-to-wall coverage begins at 6:30 p.m. ET with chief presenters Caitríona Perry, Sumi Somaskanda , and Clive Myrie .

Joining them will be Carrie Dann , managing editor of The Cook Political Report, and a panel of leading Republican and Democratic strategists.

Election Night special programming starts at 7 p.m. ET led by anchors Joe Mathieu and Kailey Leinz from global headquarters in New York. They’ll be joined by Rick Davis , Jeanne Sheehan Zaino , former representatives Patrick McHenry, Adam Hodge , Tyler Kendall , and David Gura .

Beginning at 7 p.m. ET, election night coverage hosted by Tony Dokoupil and Norah O’Donnell will air across the CBS Television Network, CBS News 24/7, and digital platforms. They will be joined on set by Gayle King , Margaret Brennan , Robert Costa, Major Garrett, Nancy Cordes , and Ed O’Keefe.

CBS News will offer a live election analysis show, Election 2026: The Nerd Show, on nonlinear platforms, hosted by Anthony Salvanto and Caitlin Huey-Burns . They will be joined by Democratic and Republican pollsters and other election data experts .

CNBC.com will debut a live blog starting at 12 p.m. ET, providing live results featuring market, investor, and economic context.

Election Night in America special coverage begins at 4 p.m. ET with Jake Tapper and Anderson Cooper co-anchoring live from Washington, D.C., joined by Dana Bash , Kaitlan Collins , Erin Burnett , John King , Boris Sanchez , David Chalian , Kasie Hunt , Pamela Brown , Laura Coates , Tom Foreman, David Axelrod , Scott Jennings , and Van Jones .

CNN All Access subscribers can stream live special election coverage and access exclusive, subscriber-only programming, including a special Election Night edition of CNN Office Hours with J ohn Berman and Harry Enten at 7 p.m. ET.

Beginning at 4 p.m., C-SPAN will deliver at least 20 continuous hours of live, commercial-free coverage and reports from more than 30 locations across the country.

The network is touting its flagship channel’s coverage as partisan-pundit-free, featuring expert, nonpartisan analysis.

On C-SPAN2 and C-SPAN3, coverage will consist of livestreams from two YouTube creators and two political perspectives: progressive and conservative.

The network’s FOX News Democracy 26 coverage will be co-anchored by Bret Baier and Martha MacCallum beginning at 6 p.m. ET. Appearing alongside them throughout the evening will be Dana Perino , Brit Hume , Harold Ford Jr. , Bill Hemmer , Sandra Smith , Laura Ingraham , Jesse Watters , Sean Hannity , Trace Gallagher , Harris Faulkner , Kayleigh McEnany , and Jessica Tarlov .

In addition, the Fox One streaming service will debut an interactive election experience featuring coverage from Fox News and Fox Local Stations. It will include a Command Center, an Election Hub, and a reimagined Ask Fox with Elections Mode.

At Fox Nation, The Ruthless Podcast, co-hosted by Josh Holmes , Michael Duncan , and John Ashbrook , along with Shashank Tripathi , will helm an election night special entitled Ruthless Live! Midterm Election Show live from 8-11 p.m.

Beginning at 6 p.m. ET, Rachel Maddow will lead primetime election coverage with Nicolle Wallace , Chris Hayes , Jen Psaki , Lawrence O’Donnell , Michael Steele , Symone Sanders Townsend , Ari Melber , Peter Alexander , and Stephanie Ruhle .

Ruhle, Eugene Daniels , Katy Tur , and Luke Russert will host MS NOW Members Lounge: Election Night Live Q&A , a three-hour interactive session at MS NOW Green Room starting at 8 p.m. ET.

Savannah Guthrie , Tom Llamas , Kristen Welker , Hallie Jackson , and Steve Kornacki will lead 13 hours of election coverage beginning at 5 p.m. ET. Ryan Nobles , Garrett Haake , and Brian Cheung will join them.

The Kornacki Cam livestream will make a return, and Gadi Schwartz will host a special mobile-first, vertical video livestream from Texas beginning at 7:30 p.m. ET.

Peacock will also offer a multiview election night experience.

Decision Desk 2026: Election Night in America will be co-anchored by Chris Cuomo , Elizabeth Vargas , Leland Vittert , Katie Pavlich , and Chris Stirewalt beginning at 7 p.m. ET.

The network will once again partner exclusively with election data provider Decision Desk HQ for independent race call information on election night.

Julio Vaqueiro and Arantxa Loizaga will anchor the network’s primetime coverage from Telemundo Center in Miami starting at 7 p.m. ET, joined by Johana Suárez, Vanessa Hauc, Damià Bonmatí , and Claudia de la Fuente.

The network will also work closely with the NBC News Decision Desk to provide minute-by-minute results and independent race calls.

Coverage will air on Telemundo and stream live on Noticias Telemundo AHORA, the Noticias Telemundo app , YouTube , TikTok , Instagram , and Facebook.

That breadth is the main reason enterprise buyers shortlist it. It is also the main reason they look elsewhere. articles.title: The Cheesecake Factory Is the Real Winner in Obama-Trump Food Fight
articles.fullContent:
By Nataly Kelly On Saturday, former President Barack Obama stood onstage in Cleveland and said the White House looked like “Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.”

By Monday night, President Donald Trump was telling voters at a rally in Mississippi that The Cheesecake Factory is “a very successful company,” and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent ate a meal there the same day.

Within days, the brand was featured on CNN, CNBC, and was covered by the Associated Press, USA Today, Fortune, and major media outlets. Google searches for The Cheesecake Factory also jumped 70% over the prior week, per Google Trends, and 130% compared to the same week a year earlier.

That’s the type of attention every CMO dreams of getting, so long as it’s positive. Many wouldn’t be able to resist seizing on being thrust into the national conversation. But The Cheesecake Factory said nothing.

The brand didn’t respond to requests for comment. When it reported earnings on Tuesday, nobody on the call mentioned Obama, Trump, or the White House. CEO David Overton stated, about younger guests, that the brand “has always had broad appeal.” Simple, and sufficient.

Both sides wanted a seat at the brand’s table

The financial results the company reported to investors this week, and the timing, could make this recent attention look like an immediate payoff. After all, the chain’s revenue topped $1 billion for a second straight record quarter, and comparable sales rose 15.2%. But none of that came from this recent interest from politicians and media.

A week of headlines might lead to earned attention. But business growth comes from years of people choosing you for dinner.

What’s far more telling than short-term share price fluctuation is the fact that both sides tried to claim a relationship with the brand.

Trump defended it as a success story. Obama, at a Georgia rally on Wednesday, said that it was his “jam for about a decade” with his daughters. Politicians can project whatever meaning they like onto a brand. Customers ultimately vote with their wallets. And they are the ones whose views matter most.

Just like the map of voters in America, Cheesecake Factory’s growth doesn’t follow clear party lines. Its newest restaurants are in Wichita and suburban Atlanta, but its biggest markets are California, Florida, and Texas. When two sides of America are fighting to own you, the only way to lose is to pick one.

Staying quiet can work, but only when your brand is strong enough to exercise restraint. The Cheesecake Factory’s was, thanks to work that took place long before any politicians ever joked about it.

Most brands can’t do this. If your customers skew hard toward one side of the aisle, silence can read as hiding, but a response can read as pandering. Identifying which of these two risks is greater requires first knowing who your customers are and how they see you.

One of the hardest moments a CMO can face is making a clear-headed decision at the very same moment when the CEO is forwarding screenshots, investors are stressed, and agencies and employees are drafting clever memes and tempting witticisms. But the people who are loud on social media are not always the ones who matter most. The opinion poll that really matters is that of the family splitting avocado egg rolls on a Tuesday night.

From my experience looking at large volumes of brand health data, the brands that know when to join the conversation and when to hold back have something in common: They know their brand, and understand what every segment of consumers think of it deeply. They track and care about awareness, consideration, and sentiment. That’s what enables them to walk into a viral media week knowing whether their brand equity can absorb it or not.

The Four Down and Dirtiest Political Ads of the 2026 Midterms The case for a wink

But even if your brand has strong brand equity, silence isn’t always the best move. There are times when humor works well, and can still be apolitical. A quip such as “Every table’s open. Even for former presidents” could have grabbed more attention, without taking sides.

But timing also matters. With only days remaining before a midterm election, The Cheesecake Factory didn’t need more attention around politics at this exact moment.

That said, when a controversy relates to how the company treats staff or guests, or makes a brand look bad, silence can read as indifference. Knowing your customers tells you whether a moment is just noise, or if it carries real risk.

Then there’s the global risk mitigation that Americans tend to forget, but global CMOs cannot. The Cheesecake Factory has licensed restaurants in Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, Mexico, mainland China, Hong Kong, Macau, and Thailand. The Saddam Hussein joke might land well in Cleveland, but perhaps not in Kuwait City. Any commentary has to be crafted carefully, to ensure it can reflect well on a brand in every market it cares about, all at once.

Every marketer wants to build a brand that culture has something to say about, so that you can decide whether or not you want to say anything back. But the goal is not only having the ability to choose. In fact, when a viral moment pulls your brand into a fight it didn’t start, the very first question to ask isn’t how, or if, to respond.

Instead, you should ask whether you know—from real data, and not just a hunch—how consumers actually see your brand. If you don’t, even the best wink-and-nod social post on the planet won’t save you.

Nataly Kelly is the chief marketing officer of Zappi.

articles.title: Week of Oct. 19 Cable News Ratings: Networks Grow in Total Viewers

By Mark Mwachiro This is TVNewser’s basic cable network ranker and cable news report for the week of October 19, 2026.

Fox News, MS NOW, and CNN gained viewers week over week in total viewers. However, MS NOW grew across the board.

CNN’s demo loss was MS NOW’s gain as the network moved ahead of the now-owned Skydance property to capture second place within that measurement.

According to Nielsen big data + panel for the week of Oct. 19, Fox News averaged 1.747 million total viewers and 140,000 A25-54 viewers during primetime. The network was up +1% in total viewers but fell by -11% in the demo compared with the prior week ( the week beginning Oct. 12 ).

During total day viewing, Fox News averaged 1.156 million total viewers and 103,000 A25-54 viewers. Based on the previous week’s average, the network grew by +5% in total viewers and the demo.

Fox News moved from third to second in total primetime viewership and remained fourth in demo viewership among all basic cable networks. During total day, it remained first in total viewers and was in third place in the total day demo.

MS NOW averaged 954,000 total viewers and 111,000 viewers in the A25-54 demo for the week that just concluded. This represented gains of +3% in total viewers and +19% in the demo compared with its primetime average the prior week.

During total day, MS NOW averaged 609,000 total viewers and 67,000 demo viewers. It was up by +2% in total viewers and +12% in the demo compared with the network’s average the prior week. It was the only network with double-digit gains in either of the measured categories.

Among all basic cable networks, MS NOW jumped to third from fifth place in total primetime viewers and was sixth in the demo. It continued to be in third in total viewers and finished in sixth place in the total day demo.

CNN averaged 632,000 total primetime viewers and 117,000 demo viewers. It was up by +1% in total viewers and +2% in the demo compared to the previous week.

During total day, the network had 424,000 total viewers and 65,000 viewers in the demo. For CNN, it gained +1% in total viewers but was down -4% in the demo during this daypart.

Among all cable networks, CNN climbed from sixth to fifth place in total viewers and was also in a similar position in the demo during primetime. It was No. 4 in total day among total viewers and remained in eighth in the demo.

When looking at these networks’ performance during the same period a year ago :

During primetime, Fox News was down -23% in total viewers and -35% in the A25-54 demo. During total day, the network was down -21% in total viewers and -26% in the demo—the only network with declines within this yearly comparison.

MS NOW was up +30% in total viewers and +79% in the demo. During total day, the network gained +28% in total viewers and +60% in the demo.

In primetime, CNN was up by +28% in total viewers and +48% in the demo. During total day, it was up by +11% in total viewers and +10% in the demo.

Fox News held 12 of the 15 spots among the week’s most-watched cable news shows, with The Five in first place with 2.794 million total viewers at 5 p.m. ET. MS NOW was represented in the chart by Monday’s 9 p.m. ET airing of The Rachel Maddow Show, with 1.806 million total viewers at No. 7. The Last Word with Lawrence O’Donnell , airing weeknights at 10 p.m. ET, took 14th place with 1.242 million total viewers. The 5 p.m. ET edition of Deadline: White House with Nicolle Wallace ranked 15th with 1.163 million total viewers.

Fox News held 11 of the 15 top spots in the Adults 25-54 demo, with The Five in the No. 1 position with 235,000 viewers. MS NOW’s The Rachel Maddow Show was in third place with 186,000 demo viewers. The other MS NOW program in the top 15 was The Last Word with Lawrence O’Donnell, averaging 145,000 viewers to take 11th place. CNN NewsNight with Abby Phillip , which airs five nights a week at 10 p.m. ET, was at No. 9 with 147,000 viewers, and CNN’s The Source with Kaitlan Collins , which airs weeknights at 9 p.m. ET, was in 12th place with 135,000 demo viewers.

articles.title: Answer Engine Optimization: How to Improve AI Visibility
articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • About 68% of U.S. Google searches now end without a click. Answer engines like ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Mode deliver results without sending users to your site.
  • Answer engine optimization (AEO) helps your content show up in AI-generated responses and voice search results.
  • AEO extends your SEO strategy by focusing on visibility in conversational and zero-click search.
  • To win in AEO, you need to optimize for direct questions, structured answers, user intent, and authority signals.
  • Google states that AEO and GEO are “still SEO.” Google’s AI features are based on the same ranking and quality systems as traditional search. Strong SEO fundamentals still matter for AI visibility on Google. 
  • Citations now drive clicks. Brands cited in Google’s AI Overviews earn 120 percent more organic clicks per impression than when they aren’t cited. 
  • AI-first search is shifting user behavior. The sooner you adapt, the more visibility you’ll protect.

More than half of searches in 2025 don’t lead anywhere. People get answers from ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews, and Gemini without clicking a single link.

Google’s AI Mode takes this even further. It turns search into a full conversation and already has more than 1 billion monthly users.

If you’re not showing up in these responses, then you’re invisible to half the internet.

That’s where answer engine optimization (AEO) comes in. It helps your brand become the answer that AI tools deliver.

AEO means optimizing for standalone AI tools like ChatGPT and Perplexity alongside Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode. Each presents results differently, so your AEO strategy needs to account for all of them.

This guide breaks down how AEO works, how it compares to search engine optimization (SEO), and how to get your content found across modern search platforms. 

What Is Answer Engine Optimization?

Answer Engine Optimization is the process of making it easier for AI-powered answer engines to find, interpret, and cite your content. It’s different from optimizing for a list of ranked links. 

Google laid the groundwork years ago with Featured Snippets and People Also Ask boxes. Today, AEO is about showing up across AI-driven answer engines like ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, and Google’s AI Overviews, as seen below.

These results still include links, but there’s no guarantee users will click them.

If you want to appear in those answers, your content needs to match how large language models (LLMs) process information. This includes:

  • Natural language clarity
  • Structured data and schema markup
  • Topical authority and entity-level signals
  • Inclusion in knowledge graphs and trusted datasets

What is social media in education?

Social media in education is the use of platforms like YouTube, Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn, Facebook, and X for teaching, learning, and institutional communication. It generally covers two distinct things, and it helps to keep them separate.

The first is social media as a classroom tool: assignments, discussion prompts, livestreamed lectures, digital literacy lessons, and collaboration between students. The second is social media as an institutional channel: recruitment campaigns, campus alerts, alumni relations, and brand building.

What are the benefits of social media in education?

Used well, social media can make classrooms more engaged and institutions more connected. The main benefits:

  • Student engagement: Reaching learners on platforms they already use
  • Global access: Connecting students with experts and perspectives beyond campus
  • Collaboration: Easier communication between students, and between students and teachers
  • Professional development: Peer learning communities for educators

How does social media increase student engagement?

Social media increases student engagement by meeting learners on platforms they already use. Normally, when we discuss “engagement,” we’re referring to likes, comments, and shares on a social media post. However, “engagement” can have a double meaning when using social media in education.

Student engagement is key to a successful classroom. When students are engaged, curious, and social in class, it shows that you are succeeding as an educator.

Social media resources can help facilitate and encourage engagement with your students. When teens are spending 1 hour and 18 minutes per day on TikTok alone, bringing those platforms into the classroom helps you meet them where they already are rather than competing for their attention.

How does social media provide access to global resources and expert perspectives?

Social media lets students connect with anyone around the world. One of the best things to come out of social media is this ability, and it has a benefit in the classroom, too, especially for higher education programs.

How does social media improve communication and collaboration?

Social media improves communication because most students are already comfortable using it. It only makes sense to bring that communication method into the classroom.

Social media can be a great way to facilitate conversations around lessons or collaborations for group projects. Think private Facebook Groups or Slack channels. Students can also build their collaborative skills with document-sharing tools like Google Docs. Groups of students can share notes and collaborate during lessons in real time.

Social media supports professional development by giving educators a low-cost way to learn from peers. Inviting, rather than resisting, social media into your classroom can have huge benefits. Use it to promote collaboration, share resources and ideas, and provide real-time feedback.

“Click link in bio” is more than a meme; it’s also a revenue driver. When optimized, your Instagram link in bio turns casual views and engagements into measurable business outcomes.

Having one clickable spot that brings together all the links for your latest social posts makes it easier for people to get to the intended destination. Plus, you no longer have to decide which five links you should add to your bio, and which one gets the top spot—your latest blog post, your new collection, your signup page?

And with Instagram’s massive user base, many of whom use it to discover and buy products, the link in bio is prime real estate to scale your traffic and conversions.

In this post, we dig deeper into how you can make the most of your Instagram link in bio, with detailed steps on how to add it and which tools to use. Let’s get started.

What is an Instagram link in bio?

An Instagram link in bio is the clickable URL displayed in the bio section of your Instagram profile. Since the platform doesn’t let you add clickable links to your captions and comments, this is the only space where you can drive direct traffic to a specific website or page.

Source: Instagram

Until 2023, Instagram limited the number of bio links to one. Now you can add up to five clickable URLs in your bio.

But there’s another catch—only the first link shows up prominently on your profile. Users have to tap to expand the section and access the rest of the links. In a world with shrinking attention spans where you have to keep your Instagram bio short and sweet, this extra step could be all the difference between someone clicking and someone tapping away.

Your Instagram link in bio centralizes and organizes all your clickable URLs, streamlining the process of driving Instagram users to your intended destination. So reach turns into results and ultimately, actual revenue.

Step 1: Go to your Instagram profile and tap on “Edit profile.”

Step 2: Tap on the “Links” section.

Step 3: Tap on “Add link” and fill out the fields with a destination URL and a relevant title. The title helps you keep track of and organize your links if you need to add multiple URLs.

Step 4: Tap on the blue check icon to go back to the “Add link” window and select it again to add a different link. Your URL will now show up in your bio, just below your profile picture.

If you have multiple links, you can also reorder the links to make sure the most relevant/recent one shows up prominently on your profile.

Similarly, the native option works well if you rely on simple funnels that don’t require complex analytics.

But for brands and creators needing to make frequent updates, a link-in-bio tool saves you the trouble of having to replace URLs every time. You get a branded landing page that you can share across multiple platforms, ensuring better consistency.

Plus, you get access to comprehensive link analytics that show you exactly which campaigns worked and which ones fell flat. You can even tie your link performance to specific posts, helping you track what type of content generates clicks and conversions.

articles.title: How to Teach Content Strategy to Stakeholders Who Don’t Speak Marketing
articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Content strategy buy-in often breaks down in translation to non-marketers, even when the strategy is sound.  
  • Lead with what your stakeholder already measures. How a strategy ties back to organizational cost, risk, or speed means more to them than marketing buzzwords. 
  • Call attention to problems or poor performance yourself. Clarify any wrong conclusions and present solutions before stakeholders have time to spiral. 
  • Name what stays the same before you name what changes, so new tactics feel familiar to your audience. 
  • General recommendations rarely get implemented. Give your audience specific action items in a portable checklist or one-pager. 

Most content strategies don’t fail on their merits. They stall out because content strategy buy-in never arrives from the person who funds the work, approves it, or executes part of it. That might be a client-side VP, your own executive team, a sales director, or a legal reviewer who has never opened your editorial calendar. 

The data supports the gap. Content Marketing Institute research ranks cross-department collaboration among the top content marketing challenges for 21 percent of B2B marketers. 

Content marketers get very good at doing the work but still struggle to convince stakeholders how necessary it is. Those are separate skills, and we need plenty of practice in both. 

If you feel like you’re failing to get the right stakeholders on side for your strategy, read on. You’ll learn how to explain content strategy to non-marketers, so they understand the rationale enough to defend it (even when you aren’t in the room). 

Teaching Is a Different Skill Than Doing

When stakeholders deny or ignore content strategy, we usually blame the audience. Leadership doesn’t get it. The client won’t listen. Sales ignored the brief (again). 

That explanation feels comfortable, but it’s not always the truth. The question is, how well are we explaining ourselves? 

The same pattern shows up in every department. A client executive, a product manager, and a compliance reviewer all evaluate your recommendation against a different set of priorities. A decision that looks obvious to a content strategist can read as a cost or a liability to someone who only thinks about content for 20 minutes a month. 

Stakeholder education in content marketing is a learnable skill, not a personality trait. Nobody is born knowing how to translate a content audit into CFO speak. You practice, watch what explanations tend to land, and adjust. Here’s what I’ve found works consistently. 

Start with the Stakes, Not the Solution

Lead with why the decision matters to the specific person in front of you, in their terms, before you name a framework or tactic. This does more for getting buy-in for content strategy than any deck you build. 

Attention follows relevance. Open with a scenario that matches your stakeholder’s priorities, then connect your recommendation to it. 

Use this same move across different audiences: 

  • A budget holder hears a content refresh as spend on something already done. Reframe it as efficiency. You’re reinvesting in assets that already earn traffic instead of funding net-new pages that take months to mature.  
  • Legal hears a byline requirement on articles as more review work eating up their time. Reframe it as attribution control. Named authors with verifiable credentials reduce the risk of unsourced claims attributed to the company. 
  • Sales hears a webpage restructure as a cosmetic change. Reframe it as speed. Clear subheads and direct answers let a rep send one link mid-deal instead of writing a custom explanation. 

Translate your content strategy into the currency your audience already trades in, then explain the specifics where you need sign-off. Most collaborators tune in if you’re covering cost, risk, or speed. 

Beyond buzzwords, root your argument in data they recognize. A content strategist lives in organic sessions, keyword rankings, and time on page. A sales leader watches pipeline contribution and deal velocity; a CFO watches customer acquisition cost and ROI. You don’t have to drop your own metrics, just connect them. Bring the organic sessions that became pipeline; tie your rankings to the deals they influenced. Pull evidence from the dashboard they already open, then draw the line from your metric to theirs. 

Defuse the Scariest Interpretation Before They Invent It

Nearly every content strategy shift arrives attached to an alarming headline. A traffic decline. A ranking drop. A platform change nobody controls. 

The Pew Research Center tracked 68,879 Google searches and found click-through fell from 15% to 8% when an AI Overview appeared. Read that insight cold in a quarterly review and your client hears one message: our investment is evaporating. 

Speak to those concerns before they raise them. State the numbers plainly, then correct potential wrong conclusions immediately. Something like this works: “organic clicks are getting harder to win on informational queries as search engine trends shift, which is why we’re moving effort toward pages that convert and toward becoming the source these systems cite.” 

Skipping an uncomfortable number doesn’t make it disappear. Your audience fills in the blank themselves, usually with something worse than reality, and you find out during Q&A after you’ve lost the floor.

articles.fullContent:
For brands, social media is a goldmine of real-time insight into consumers’ preferences, behaviors and motivations. And segmenting social users intentionally—using live conversation data rather than static demographic details—empowers leaders to make smarter business decisions, whether it’s optimizing spend, discovering new markets or driving revenue.

But social media audience segmentation isn’t a one‑off marketing exercise. It’s a dynamic, cyclical process designed to spot emerging opportunities and inform data-grounded strategies.

With the help of this guide, you can better understand how to approach social media audience segmentation and use it to make an impact across the business.

What is social media audience segmentation?

Social media audience segmentation is the process of breaking down your target audience that’s engaging on social networks into smaller, distinct groups based on shared characteristics, behaviors or interests.

In contrast to broader marketing segmentation, social segmentation draws on real-time social data. Think live conversation, engagement and sentiment data, rather than CRM or survey inputs that may reflect the past and not a user’s present feelings.

Segmentation is one of the many pillars of social media intelligence, helping organizations move beyond broad audience assumptions by uncovering the distinct groups driving conversations online. Teams can then make more targeted decisions aligned to the current pulse of the market across customer care, product innovation, campaign planning and overall business strategy.

Why audience segmentation matters more than ever

One of the key factors driving the need for segmentation is the degradation of trust and attention among consumers.

According to the Q1 2026 Sprout Pulse Survey, consumers are becoming more particular about what they engage with online, with two-thirds (66%) feeling more selective than a year ago. AI slop (i.e. undifferentiated, one-size-fits-all content) was cited as a contributor to eroding trust; 56% of respondents said they see AI slop often or very often.

Many brands are mistakenly investing in this generic content. This ultimately results in wasted budget as platforms are increasingly rewarding relevance over reach.

Segmentation is what enables brands to achieve personalization and, in turn, resonance with their audiences—without necessarily needing to increase headcount or budget.

4 types of social media audience segments (and where social data fits)

Let’s take a look at four key types of social media audience segments, what they tell you and the social signals that paint the picture of who they are.

Demographic segmentation

Basic demographics like age, gender or follower count are a reasonable starting point in creating social media segments. This data is garnered via self-disclosure (i.e. a user inputs this information when creating a profile), network-level audience demographics reported by ad managers or analytics tools.

While these details don’t tell you much on their own, they can reveal behavioral trends. For instance, you may see a generational skew depending on the networks and content formats a person engages with. In general, Instagram Reels and TikToks attract a younger audience, while Facebook’s most active users skew older.

However, it’s important to note that demographics don’t provide the soundest basis for segmentation because the data is often self-reported. Users may skip fields or deliberately enter false details to protect their privacy or access age-restricted content.

Demographic-based targeting is also losing its predictive power. Per the 2026 Influencer Marketing Report, only 17% of consumers check follower count before following a creator. For nearly half of respondents (47%), things like content topic and behavior matter far more.

With that in mind, demographics should be used as a starting point rather than a primary segmentation driver. Instead of examining people’s surface-level traits, look at the things they say and do unprompted on social. These signals are more dynamic and indicative of how people identify themselves.

Psychographic segmentation

Psychographics is the classification of people based on psychological criteria—such as values, attitudes or motivations—that influence their engagement and consumption patterns.

To segment your social audience by psychographics, review their comments, posts and shares. The content they post or engage with can tell you a lot about their internal beliefs. Your brand can then use these insights to tailor its content and target these users more closely.

For example, if your audience members regularly post about climate change and sustainability, you can place them into an environmentally motivated segment. From there, you can center your messaging around subjects related to your brand, like ethically sourced materials, reusable products or community initiatives.

Behavioral segmentation on social

While psychographics focus on what users believe, behavioral segmentation shines a light on how they behave on social. The actions they take, the conversations they partake in and the content formats they engage with.

To build behavioral segments, brands must observe audiences’ patterns. How often do they post? What formats do they share (e.g. static images, carousels, Reels)? What are they talking about in comment sections? Whose posts are they commenting on?

Finding the answers to these questions can unearth important information about consumers’ decision-making and motivations. In addition to seeing how people behave, you’ll begin to understand why. You won’t just see who they interact with, but who they really are behind the screen.

Say you identify a segment of users consistently participating in giveaways, promo codes and engaging with shopping-on-a-budget content. With this data, you can glean what might be most important to them when making purchase decisions: fair pricing and discount offers. From there, you can tailor your social messaging accordingly, whether it’s highlighting affordable prices or sharing the outsized value of your offerings.

Geographic segmentation

A person’s physical location shapes their social and spending habits—and the two often go hand in hand.

Various social signals enable brands to glean a user’s whereabouts, including location tags, geotagged posts and stories, and the language or dialect they use on social. Additionally, some network behaviors and preferences are region-specific.

articles.title: Social media leadership skills for 2026 (+ KPIs to track)
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Social media leadership skills combine strategic thinking, emotional intelligence, AI fluency, and cross-functional communication to guide enterprise teams toward business outcomes.
  2. The biggest shift in 2026 is leading AI adoption responsibly, balancing speed and governance without losing the human element.
  3. Strong social leaders measure success through team health, brand reputation, and business impact, not vanity metrics.
  4. Developing social media leadership skills requires structured feedback, clear decision-making frameworks, and a willingness to experiment and fail fast.

What are social media leadership skills?

Social media leadership skills are a blend of abilities, both learned and innate, that help leaders direct and inspire social media teams to succeed. They matter at every scale, but they matter most in enterprise environments where one decision can ripple across dozens of markets.

The core skills include:

  • Strategic thinking: Connecting social activity to business goals like revenue, retention, and reputation, rather than treating channels as standalone projects.
  • Emotional intelligence: Reading the room internally and externally, spotting burnout early, and handling sensitive moments without defensiveness.
  • Communication aptitude: Explaining social performance in language the C-suite, legal, and frontline teams all understand.
  • AI fluency: Knowing which tasks to hand to AI, which to keep human, and how to govern the output.
  • Adaptability: Shifting plans quickly when platforms, policies, or culture change without losing the thread of the strategy.
  • Creativity and innovative thinking: Creating room for teams to test new formats, including the ones that look strange on a slide.
  • Collaboration and conflict management: Navigating competing stakeholder priorities and saying no when the request does not serve the strategy.

A successful social media leader’s skills must go beyond social media management. A true leader understands how to delegate and guide in real time through an evolving industry and culture. They know how to use a social strategy to achieve business goals.

It’s no surprise, then, that a recent IBM study found 69% of CEO respondents say their organization’s success is directly tied to maintaining a broad group of leaders with a deep understanding of strategy and the authority to make critical decisions. Social is no exception.

Shakivla Todd, a 4-time Shorty award-winning Social Media Strategist, says a great social leader must be “naturally culturally aware and in-the-know.”

“You don’t need to be chronically online. But you do need to be acutely aware of what’s happening as it pertains to current events and cultural moments.”

Cultural relevance isn’t just to stay ‘on trend,’ says Todd. It’s to “help lead your team through culturally sensitive moments. An exceptional social media leader should know how to read the damn room, everyone hates a tone-deaf brand.”

In short: social media leadership skills are the mix of strategic, human, and technical abilities that turn a capable social team into a business function executives rely on.

How is social media leadership different from management?

Social media leadership sets the direction; social media management executes against it. Both roles are essential, and most leaders have done both, but the day-to-day work looks very different.

Social media managers focus on executing a social media strategy. Their social tasks include:

  • Creating and publishing compelling content
  • Understanding how social networks like LinkedIn, TikTok, or Instagram work
  • Engaging an audience
  • Analyzing and optimizing performance
  • Maintaining brand voice

Social media leaders, on the other hand, set a direction and keep everyone working toward it. They:

  • Shape the long-term vision
  • Advocate for resources
  • Build systems that allow their teams to move quickly while staying aligned

A manager might be optimizing a campaign’s engagement rate. A leader is the one asking how that engagement ladders up to revenue, reputation, and retention.

In social, business leaders have to stay flexible. The industry changes fast, and you need to be able to pivot, using new trends and real data, to build initiatives that actually move the business forward.

“Keeping up with the swiftness of social media is an Olympic sport,” says Todd. “I’ve learned to be comfortable with uncertainty, and I don’t get too attached to plans.”

What does a social media director do?

A social media director sits between management and leadership, owning the strategic direction of social while staying close enough to the work to guide it. The role is usually where social media leadership skills get tested for the first time at scale.

Typical social media director responsibilities include:

  • Strategy ownership: Setting the annual social strategy and making sure every channel maps to a business objective.
  • Team oversight: Hiring, structuring, and developing the social team, including agency and freelance partners.
  • Budget and resourcing: Building the business case for headcount, tools, and paid support.
  • Executive reporting: Translating social performance into the metrics leadership already tracks.

What are the newest Instagram features in 2026?

The newest Instagram features focus on video editing, profile control, and resharing other people’s content. Here’s what’s landed most recently, and why each one matters for marketing teams. For ongoing changes, we track every release in our Instagram updates hub.

  • The Edits video editing app

Instagram Edits app

Instagram Edits is a standalone video editing app Instagram launched in 2025. It includes a project timeline, a teleprompter for scripted pieces, audio and beat alignment tools, and performance insights for the videos you export.

For marketers, the appeal is practical: you can take a Reel from idea to finished edit without buying a separate editing tool, then publish straight to Instagram.

Longer Reels

Instagram has extended how long a Reel can run, giving brands room for tutorials, product walkthroughs, and short interviews that previously had to be chopped into parts.

Longer doesn’t automatically mean better. Use the extra runway only when the story needs it, and watch your retention curve to see where people drop off.

Customizable profile grids

You can now rearrange the posts on your profile grid instead of being stuck with reverse-chronological order. The grid also displays in a taller, vertical format.

This turns your profile into something closer to a landing page. Pin your best-performing or most on-message posts to the top three rows, since that’s what a new visitor sees before deciding whether to follow.

Native reposting

Instagram added an official repost button, so you can share someone else’s public Reel or feed post to your own audience with attribution built in. Reposts appear in a dedicated tab on your profile rather than mixing into your main grid.

It’s a clean way to amplify user-generated content and partner posts without screenshots or third-party repost apps.

Instagram Plus subscription

Instagram Plus is a paid subscription tier that bundles extra customization, early access to features, and additional insights. It’s aimed at heavy users and creators rather than large brand teams.

articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • The 4 Ps (product, price, place, and promotion) are tools marketers use in combination to shape how a product (or range of products) is positioned, promoted, and sold to a specific group of customers. Together, they’re often referred to as the “marketing mix.”
  • The marketing mix is fundamentally a tech-agnostic framework for helping with important marketing decisions. 
  • “Product” looks at how well features meet needs, “price” at what customers are willing and able to pay, “place” at the best ways to distribute a product, and “promotion” at building market awareness. 
  • Well-known companies like Rolex, McDonald’s, and Red Bull have perfected the 4 Ps behind their products and brand identities.
  • AI is changing how marketers execute the 4 Ps, but the fundamental questions behind product, price, place, and promotion remain the same.

The 4 Ps of marketing (product, price, place, and promotion) have been around for decades, and they still drive decisions around every successful product launch.

Also known as the “marketing mix,” they help you think through how to bring a product to market and reach the customers most likely to buy it.

It doesn’t matter if you’re running a one-person small business or a global enterprise. The 4 Ps help you bring a product to market and get it in front of people most likely to buy it.

How you put the 4 Ps to work has changed, though. AI is giving marketers new ways to understand their customers and make more informed decisions, often in less time.

I’ll cover some of these opportunities as I show you how the 4 Ps still drive marketing decision-making today.

What Are the Four Elements of the Marketing Mix?

The 4 Ps of marketing, commonly known as the marketing mix, stand for product, place, price, and promotion. They’re like four levers companies can adjust to better position their products for the customers they want to reach.

Here’s the meaning behind each of the four Ps: 

  • Product: What you’re selling, including its features, packaging, and the support that comes with it
  • Price: What you charge and how you structure the pricing
  • Place: Where and how your customers can buy the product
  • Promotion: How you get the word out about the product

To more fully understand the 4 Ps of advertising, we need to take a step back. Mention “marketing,” and most people think of customer-facing content like ads, social media posts, emails, videos, and blog articles like this one. 

In fact, these represent just one piece of a much broader discipline. They’re the “promotion” part of the mix called marketing communications.

True marketing is a big-picture process that strives to meet all customer needs. And thinking in terms of the 4 Ps allows companies to do exactly that. 

What About the 7 Ps and the 4 Cs?

The idea of a marketing mix has been around longer than the 4 Ps themselves.

In 1948, Harvard professor James Culliton described marketing executives as “mixer(s) of ingredients.” Inspired by this idea, fellow Harvard professor Neil Borden often referred to the concept of the marketing mix in the years that followed. 

Then in 1960, marketing professor E. Jerome McCarthy organized it into the four elements we know today in his book Basic Marketing: A Managerial Approach.

Other models have been suggested in the years since, with two in particular gaining traction: the 7 Ps and the 4 Cs:

  • The 7 Ps: In 1981, marketing professors Bernard Booms and Mary Jo Bitner expanded the 4 Ps to better suit service-based businesses. Their model adds people, process, and physical evidence to the mix. These cover the employees who deliver a service, the delivery process, and the environment where business takes place. 
  • The 4 Cs: Marketing professor Robert Lauterborn proposed a more customer-oriented alternative to the 4 Ps in 1990. His model replaces them with consumer wants and needs, cost, convenience, and communication. Instead of starting with what a business wants to sell, the 4 Cs push marketers to focus on what customers actually need. 

These alternative models add some useful nuance. To me, though, the 4 Ps still make up the strongest foundation for marketing campaigns. A social media dashboard is a single interface that pulls metrics from all your social accounts into one place for tracking, analyzing, and reporting on performance.

articles.title: How to build your social media team for the future of marketing
articles.fullContent:
It’s certainly not 2010 anymore. So why are so many businesses still resourcing social media teams as if it is?

Social teams have evolved far beyond publishing posts and responding to comments. Today, they manage content and video production, influencer partnerships, customer care, social search, paid media, community engagement and increasingly, social intelligence. Social’s role is expanding across the business, and a social team’s structure needs to evolve with it.

Organizations are also looking to social data for more than marketing insights. According to Sprout’s Social Intelligence Report, 93% of leaders view social intelligence as essential for future growth, yet only 10% of organizations have embedded it into enterprise strategy. Closing that gap requires more support for social teams that are already stretched across a growing list of responsibilities. They need the right people, roles and processes to turn social data into action across the business while creating more capacity for strategic work.

There’s no one-size-fits-all social media team structure. But the strongest teams connect their work directly to business outcomes rather than organizing solely around the tasks they complete. Building for that future requires the right mix of specialized expertise, cross-functional relationships and technology to keep pace with social’s expanding role.

In this guide, we’ll break down how to structure a social media team, which roles to prioritize and how to build and manage a team that’s prepared for the future of marketing.

How to structure a social media team

Social’s dynamic nature can give marketers a professional advantage if leaders give them space to grow. With the right structure, teams can quickly refine and grow their skills, creating career-making opportunities.

Proactively experimenting with new social media department structures can also shift a brand’s trajectory—helping it win a larger audience, build customer loyalty and sustain growth.

Here are four common models to consider, plus how your structure may evolve as your company grows.

1. Functional

The functional model organizes social media team roles around specific responsibilities, such as influencer partnerships, social media intelligence or paid media. Generalists may also have defined focus areas, including content creation, video production and social search optimization (SOSEO).

At Sprout, the social team also partners closely with Brand Creative on asset development and with teams across the organization—including PR, Content, Customer Marketing, Events, Internal Comms, Revenue Marketing and Product Marketing—on messaging, research and distribution.

Constantly switching between incoming DMs, reporting, influencer coordination and content production can limit time for creative and strategic thinking. A functional structure can help reduce burnout, clarify ownership and create more room for social marketers to deepen their expertise.

With clearer focus areas, teams can scale priority initiatives and measure their impact more effectively. This model works especially well for organizations that want to support career development while assigning clear ownership to specific social priorities.

2. Network

Some teams align individual employees to specific networks, such as TikTok, Instagram, Facebook or LinkedIn. With this approach, each person owns a network strategy from development through execution, which in turn enables them to build deep network expertise.

Sprout’s social team experimented with a network-specific structure in 2022 before eventually moving away from it. While the model supported highly intentional content and stronger network-specific audience insights, it wasn’t scalable for a growing team.

The social landscape has also become more fluid since network-based structures first gained popularity. New networks emerge and consumer preferences change rapidly, creating gaps or redundancies when roles are tied too closely to individual networks.

A network-based social structure can still work as an interim model for lean teams developing their social media marketing strategy from the ground up. As the team grows, shifting toward functional ownership can make it easier to adapt across networks.

3. Audience engagement

Another common team structure organizes social media team roles around audience engagement goals and customer needs. These typically fall into three categories:

  • Awareness: Creating content to increase brand visibility among new and existing audiences.
  • Engagement: Creating content and responding to comments, DMs and other inbound interactions to build community and strengthen brand loyalty.
  • Customer Service: Managing customer questions, requests and complaints to resolve issues quickly.

These teams often include specialists beyond content and community management. For example, an awareness-focused team might include a content creator, an influencer marketing strategist and a performance analyst who work together to develop relevant and effective content.

Because this model requires employees to work across multiple networks, centralized social media management software becomes especially important. Bringing publishing, engagement, reporting and collaboration into one system reduces time spent switching between disconnected platforms.

4. Center of excellence

In a social media center of excellence (CoE) model, representatives from different departments form a central council that shapes social strategy and establishes shared standards.

Participants may include leaders from PR, employer brand, HR, product, customer care and other teams that rely on or contribute to social. Together, they align priorities, improve information sharing and create clearer governance around how the organization uses social.

CoE models tend to work best for large organizations with social stakeholders spread across multiple departments or regions. A centralized group reduces silos and gives distributed teams a shared framework for decision-making, measurement and execution.

5. Structure by company size

Company size can help determine which structure makes the most sense, but complexity is often the better signal. A lean team may work well with broad ownership until the volume of channels, stakeholders and social data becomes difficult for a few people to manage.

As demand grows, teams usually need more specialization and clearer ownership. Enterprise organizations also need stronger governance, especially when social intelligence spans multiple departments. What does it mean to measure employee advocacy success?

Measuring employee advocacy success means evaluating your program’s business impact through key performance indicators (KPIs). A complete measurement approach tracks:

  • Reach and brand visibility: How far employee posts extend your brand beyond corporate channels
  • Engagement: Whether audiences are interacting with employee-shared content
  • Employee participation: How many employees are actively sharing, and how often
  • Business impact: This includes leads, conversions, hires, and ad spend saved

Tracking results turns fluffy numbers into evidence you can take to leadership. And with the right data, you can sharpen your strategy into a repeatable advocacy machine.

Real-world example: Victoria Samways, Marketing & Brand Manager at Major Tom, used employee advocacy measurement to prove a three-figure ROI on a single campaign.

  • The approach: Samways paired employee advocacy software with UTM tracking codes, then encouraged employees to share campaign content.
  • The result: Advocacy landed in Major Tom’s top 5 traffic sources for the campaign, generated over $100k in pipeline, and delivered a higher-than-average win rate.

“Thanks to the UTM tracking links, over the coming weeks, we saw a healthy amount of leads that we attributed back to this campaign,” Samways shares. “This resulted in over $100k in our pipeline and, as a channel, provided a higher-than-average win rate due to the referral-like context of these leads.”

Why is it important to measure employee advocacy success?

Measurement matters because advocacy programs compete for budget, attention, and headcount like every other initiative. Without data, they almost always lose that competition.

Here are three specific risks of running an unmeasured employee advocacy program:

  1. You can’t defend your budget. Measurement shows how your program moves the needle on reach, leads, and recruiting.
  2. You can’t fix what’s broken. Without data, you don’t know if low participation is a content problem, a platform problem, or a culture problem.
  3. You can’t replicate what’s working. Measurement shows you which campaigns, content types, and brand advocates are driving the strongest results. When you know what’s working, you can streamline your efforts and scale the wins.

There’s another upside that’s easy to underestimate: measurement makes employees take the program more seriously. And with 2026 social trends pointing to ROI as the defining factor of ambassador programs, that rigor has never been more important.

When employee advocates can see their own impact, they participate more and stick with the program longer. In other words, the act of measuring is itself a participation lever.

The bottom line: A social media post that racks up a thousand likes feels great, but if those likes aren’t turning into top talent, qualified leads, or customers, what’s the point? Measurement is what makes the impact of employee advocacy visible.

You build an employee advocacy measurement framework by deciding what the program is meant to achieve, then choosing the employee advocacy KPIs that map to each goal. Doing this first saves you from drowning in metrics that nobody in the business cares about.

  3. Set your baselines: Record where each metric sits before the program launches (or before your next big push). Without a baseline, you have numbers but no story.
  4. Agree on a reporting cadence: Review participation and engagement monthly so you can course-correct quickly. Save business impact metrics like pipeline and earned media value for quarterly reviews.

articles.title: How to Use Facebook Groups for Marketing
articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Facebook’s ranking system treats Group posts differently from Page posts, which can extend your business’s reach within a Group.
  • A strong marketing strategy uses Facebook Pages for wide visibility and Groups for deeper community engagement.
  • Learning how to grow a Facebook Group starts with broad, creative-first Facebook ads. It’s no longer about the granular interest-stacking that used to work.
  • Membership questions help you qualify leads up front, and consistent value posts keep them engaged long enough to sell privately (not in the Group feed).
  • You can monetize Groups in various ways, but only once the community is established and users understand the Group’s value. 

Marketers rely on good strategy to reach their target audiences, and one of those strategies is harnessing the power of Facebook Groups. 

With more than 3 billion monthly active users, 1.8 billion of whom participate in Facebook Groups, these online communities are great places to engage with your audience.

Facebook Groups are where users connect over common interests. For your business, that means direct access to people who already want to hear from you. That kind of engagement can boost your brand and give you valuable insights about your audience. 

This guide will cover how to use Facebook Groups for marketing strategies. You’ll learn how to grow your audience, generate leads, measure results, and monetize your Group.

Let’s get started.

Why Facebook Groups Work for Marketing

Two things make Facebook Groups effective for marketing: how the algorithm treats Group content, and the kind of audience that shows up to participate.

  • Algorithm advantage. Facebook’s own Feed Ranking documentation confirms Groups get a dedicated ranking system that is designed for community engagement. Some businesses that use Groups may reach a higher share of users than just posting in their feed. Meta’s Widely Viewed Content Report for Q1 2026 shows that over 14 percent of posts users see are from their Groups.
  • Opt-in audience quality. Joining a Group is a more deliberate action and a stronger signal of intent than liking a Page because users are choosing to enter a community, not just like your Page. Black Friday prep is happening earlier than ever for shoppers this year. Your customers are already looking for deals online and increasingly on social media. According to a Q3 2026 Sprout Social Pulse Survey, 78% of users plan to use social as much or more than they did last year to help them find and purchase gifts this year.

If you want to make the most of Black Friday on social media, start planning your strategy now. Customers are eager for ideas well before November.

5 types of Black Friday social media posts (+ examples)

Spurred by the growth of online shopping and social commerce, Black Friday has become a multi-day event, including Small Business Saturday and Cyber Monday. According to the data, customers are thinking about their holiday shopping differently this year, and ecommerce is a key part of their plans.

More than half of respondents (69%) to the Q3 2026 pulse survey said they’re concerned about rising prices due to tariffs. Over a third (36%) are planning to shop earlier to specifically avoid tariff-related price jumps, and 56% are planning to reduce their holiday spending overall due to economic conditions.

For brands, that means competition is higher and earning customer trust will take more legwork. To create a winning Black Friday marketing strategy, it’s crucial to tap into the power of social.

Nearly a quarter (23%) of the Q3 pulse survey respondents said the quality of a company’s social media customer service makes them more likely to purchase this holiday season, and a similar percentage said the originality of holiday-specific social content makes a difference. Here are different types of Black Friday social media posts that have worked for other brands to inspire your campaign planning.

Influencer collaborations

Partner with influencers to create tailored content for specific demographics. From fashion lovers to tech enthusiasts, influencers can connect with high-intent niche audiences. If your Black Friday deals are perfect for a particular type of customer, working with influencers who already speak to that crowd can build trust and revenue

Offering special discounts and promo codes via influencers is one way to track ROI of a campaign and boost sales. In fact, promo codes are the leading factor influencing the purchasing decisions of social media scrollers. Thirty percent of respondents to the Q3 pulse survey said promo codes influencers share make them more likely to purchase from a brand during the holidays, more than any other factor in the survey.

Keep in mind that follower count is not the main barometer of impact for your influencer partnerships. Instead, focus on social media discoverability. Working with influencers who can create hyper-relevant content is key to getting your campaign seen by new audiences. Small businesses with modest budgets and larger companies alike can embrace micro-influencer marketing this gifting season.

For example, Rilee Smith, a travel and packing influencer on Instagram, crafted a video in partnership with five of her favorite bag brands to offer her followers a slate of Black Friday sales. Her video showed each of the bags in action and what discounts the brands offered.

Giveaways and contests

Grab consumer attention by giving away free merchandise. Create a social media giveaway or contest to improve your engagement and supercharge the buzz around your brand.

Giveaways and contests boost your follower count, convert leads, amplify brand awareness and increase loyalty.

The result was promotion of the giveaway and the broader discounts available for the shopping-centric weekend.

Want to incentivize your audience to return to your website or shop with you after Black Friday ends? Promote your rewards or loyalty program. These programs typically offer discounts, coupons or early access to repeat shoppers—all of which encourage brand loyalty.

The cost savings loyalty programs offer are especially appealing to customers this year and create a way to build trust with your audience. Discounts, special social content and exclusive savings for your loyalty members show them you know their discretionary dollars are valuable, and you’re willing to go the extra mile to keep them coming back.

Luggage brand SWISSGEAR offered their rewards members early access to a 60% off Black Friday sale. Customers looking to plan their holiday purchases as early as possible this year will appreciate a first shot at discounts and bundles. Your social channels are a useful tool alongside email marketing to let members know about exclusive benefits for the holidays.

That shift has important implications for content teams, particularly as AI changes how audiences discover and evaluate information.

The opportunity isn’t simply to produce more content with AI. Brands need systems that connect audience insights, human expertise, content creation, distribution, and performance measurement. The teams that build these processes can continuously improve their content while adapting to changing audience behavior and search environments.

McKinsey’s research points to a broader change in marketing: AI is moving teams away from isolated campaigns and toward a continuously improving growth engine.

Traditional campaigns are usually planned around a defined launch, run for a set period, and evaluated afterward.

articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Websites remain an important way for consumers to verify that a business is legitimate.
  • Wix’s State of Websites report found that search still accounts for 42% of website traffic.
  • Sites with structured data that passes Google’s rich-results inspection earn 2x more revenue and 9x more traffic than sites without it.
  • Blogs and reviews can strengthen a brand’s authority and contribute to business growth.
  • As AI changes discovery, a credible website can give consumers and AI systems a reliable source of information about a brand.

AI has made it easier than ever to create a website, generate content, and put a brand online. That speed comes with a new challenge: consumers have more reason to question what they see.

A convincing business can appear online almost overnight. For customers, a website therefore has an important job beyond selling products or services. It can help establish that a business is real.

Wix’s first State of Websites report, based on data from more than 300 million users, examines how websites are being built, discovered, and used in the age of AI. The report found that websites remain central to business growth, even as discovery expands across AI platforms and other channels.

For marketers, the takeaway is straightforward. Website credibility still matters. The challenge is making sure a website provides the information, content, and technical signals that support trust with both people and machines.

Why Websites Still Matter in the Age of AI

AI search is changing how people find information, but it hasn’t eliminated the need for a destination where customers can verify what they’ve learned.

Source

Websites Help Consumers Verify a Business

Wix’s research describes a growing tension around AI and website creation. Building a site is becoming faster, but customers still need confidence that a business is legitimate.

A consumer might discover a company through an AI recommendation, social platform, or traditional search result. Before making a purchase or contacting the business, they may visit its website to confirm that the company exists and learn more about what it offers.

That makes a website part of the validation process.

A professional domain, clear business information, useful content, customer reviews, and evidence of expertise can all contribute to website trust. These signals help answer a basic question that becomes increasingly important as AI-generated information becomes easier to produce: Is this business real?

AI Search Is Changing Discovery, Not Replacing Websites

The Wix report found that AI platforms are increasingly interacting with websites. Its data shows that LLMs still account for less than 1% of website traffic, although traffic from LLMs grew fourfold between 2024 and 2025.

Traditional search remains much more significant. Search accounts for 42% of traffic to Wix sites, compared with 40% from direct traffic and 13% from social.

This puts the current state of discovery into perspective. AI search is growing quickly, but traditional search continues to be a major source of website visits.

For brands, that means the website still needs to serve both audiences: people arriving directly or through search and AI systems looking for information to use in their responses.

What the Wix Data Says About Website Trust

The report highlights several website characteristics associated with stronger business performance.


Source

Structured Data Can Support Visibility

One of the clearest findings concerns structured data.

Wix found that sites with structured data markup that passed Google’s rich-results inspection earned 2x more revenue and received 9x more traffic than sites without it.

This is a correlation in Wix’s dataset, not evidence that adding structured data directly causes those outcomes. Still, the finding reinforces the importance of making website information easier for search engines and AI systems to understand.

Structured data gives machines additional context about the information presented on a page. As search experiences become more sophisticated, that machine-readable layer can help make important information easier to interpret.

For brands investing in AI visibility, technical foundations such as structured data should therefore remain part of the conversation.
